cards.text: The universe is transformation; life is opinion.
cards.meaning: Events themselves are neutral and always changing. What makes something feel like a disaster or a win is the judgment you attach to it, and that part is yours to control.
cards.apply: Next time something goes wrong at work, write down the bare facts in one line, then the story you're telling yourself. Act on the facts.

cards.text: No longer talk at all about the kind of man that a good man ought to be, but be such.
cards.meaning: Marcus is impatient with himself: philosophising about virtue is a way to avoid practising it. Character shows up in what you do today, not in what you believe.
cards.apply: Pick one value you talk about a lot (say, candour) and do one concrete thing that expresses it before the day ends.

cards.text: Take the view from above
cards.meaning: Marcus repeatedly zooms out: picture the whole earth, the length of history, the thousands of people who've had this exact problem. From that height, most worries shrink to their real size.
cards.apply: When you're stressed about a deadline or a bad call, ask: will this matter in five years? Then decide how much energy it actually deserves.

cards.text: Focus only on what is up to you
cards.meaning: Your judgments, intentions and actions are in your control; other people's opinions, markets and outcomes are not. Spending energy on the second group is how you lose peace of mind.
cards.apply: Split your current worry list into two columns, 'mine' and 'not mine', and only make plans for the first column.

cards.text: It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it.
cards.meaning: Life feels short because we spend it carelessly: on busywork, other people's agendas and postponing what matters. Used well, the time we have is long enough.
cards.apply: Audit last week's calendar. Mark each block as chosen or defaulted-into, and cut one recurring defaulted block.

cards.text: People guard their money but give away their time
cards.meaning: Seneca notes that nobody lets strangers take their property, yet everyone lets others take their hours, the one asset that can never be earned back.
cards.apply: Before accepting the next meeting or favour, ask what you'd be willing to pay in cash to skip it. Say no if the answer is 'a lot'.

cards.text: Stop postponing your life
cards.meaning: Planning to really live 'after the next promotion' or 'at retirement' bets on a future you aren't promised. Seneca calls postponement the biggest waste of life.
cards.apply: Name one thing you keep saving for 'someday' and schedule a small version of it within the next 30 days.

cards.text: All warfare is based on deception.
cards.meaning: In any contest, controlling what the other side knows and believes is a weapon. Appearing weak when strong, or far when near, shapes the opponent's choices.
cards.apply: In a negotiation, decide in advance what you won't reveal (your walk-away price, your timeline) and stick to it.

cards.text: The victorious strategist only seeks battle after the victory has been won.
cards.meaning: Winners set up the conditions for success beforehand: preparation, position and information. The actual fight just confirms what's already decided.
cards.apply: Before your next big meeting or pitch, list the three hardest questions you could get and have the answers ready.

cards.text: If you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles.
cards.meaning: Good decisions need an honest read of both sides: the other party's goals and limits, and your own strengths and blind spots. Missing either half leads to defeats you should have seen coming.
cards.apply: For a current competitor or counterparty, write one paragraph on what they want most and one on where you're weakest.

cards.text: Mr. Market is your moody business partner
cards.meaning: Graham pictures the market as a partner who shows up every day offering to buy or sell at prices that swing with his mood. You're free to ignore him, and to use his panics and euphoria to your advantage.
cards.apply: Write down your estimate of value and your buy/sell levels before you look at today's price, not after.

cards.text: Always demand a margin of safety
cards.meaning: Buy only when the price is well below a conservative estimate of value. The gap absorbs errors, bad luck and forecasts that don't pan out.
cards.apply: In your next model, stress your key assumptions (exit multiple, growth, cost of capital) and check whether the deal still works at the downside case.

cards.text: The investor's chief problem—and even his worst enemy—is likely to be himself.
cards.meaning: Most investing mistakes come from behaviour, not analysis: chasing what's hot, panicking in drawdowns, overconfidence. Controlling yourself matters more than being clever.
cards.apply: Keep a short decision journal: for each trade or call, note your reasoning and emotional state, and review it monthly.

cards.text: Invert, always invert.
cards.meaning: Borrowed from the mathematician Jacobi: many problems are easier solved backwards. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid it.
cards.apply: Run a pre-mortem on your current project or position: imagine it failed badly a year from now and list the reasons why.

cards.text: Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.
cards.meaning: People respond to how they're rewarded far more than to what they're told. If you want to predict or change behaviour, look at the incentives first.
cards.apply: For any recommendation you get (a broker, a sponsor, a vendor), ask how that person gets paid if you say yes.

cards.text: Build a latticework of mental models
cards.meaning: Munger argues that knowing the big ideas from many fields (psychology, economics, maths, biology) beats deep knowledge of one. Each model catches errors the others miss.
cards.apply: Pick one model from outside finance this month (for example, feedback loops or base rates) and apply it to a decision you're making.

cards.text: Two systems run your mind
cards.meaning: System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive; System 2 is slow, effortful and logical. Most errors come from System 1 answering a question that needed System 2.
cards.apply: For any decision above a set size, force a pause: write the decision and your reasoning down before committing.

cards.text: What you see is all there is
cards.meaning: The mind builds a confident story from whatever information is in front of it and rarely asks what's missing. Fewer facts can even make a story feel more coherent.
cards.apply: Before finalising a view, add a line to your notes: 'What would I need to know that I don't?'

cards.text: Take the outside view
cards.meaning: We plan from the inside, imagining how our project will unfold, and end up too optimistic. The fix is to look at how similar projects actually turned out (the base rate).
cards.apply: When estimating a timeline or budget, first find how long comparable efforts really took, then adjust from there.

cards.text: Behaviour beats intelligence with money
cards.meaning: Housel's core point: financial success depends more on how you act (patience, restraint, avoiding ruin) than on how smart you are. A modest earner with discipline can beat a genius with no self-control.
cards.apply: Automate one good money behaviour this week, like a fixed transfer to savings or investments on payday.

cards.text: Compounding needs time more than skill
cards.meaning: Housel points out that most of Warren Buffett's fortune was built after his mid-60s. The real edge was investing well for an extraordinarily long time.
cards.apply: Look at your plans and ask what would make you interrupt compounding (forced selling, too much leverage), and remove that risk.

cards.text: Know when you have enough
cards.meaning: The hardest financial skill is getting the goalposts to stop moving. Risking what you have and need for what you don't need is how people blow up.
cards.apply: Write down a concrete number or lifestyle that would count as 'enough', and use it to judge new risks.

cards.text: Fix your systems, not your goals
cards.meaning: Winners and losers often share the same goals. What separates them is the daily process. Goals set direction; systems produce results.
cards.apply: Take one goal you have and rewrite it as a daily or weekly routine you can actually repeat.

cards.text: Every action is a vote for who you are
cards.meaning: Lasting change is identity-based: you stop trying to 'read more' and start being 'a reader'. Each small action is evidence for that identity.
cards.apply: Pick the identity you want (for example, 'someone who trains') and do a tiny version of it today, even two minutes.

cards.text: 1% better every day adds up
cards.meaning: Small improvements compound. Improving 1% a day for a year multiplies out to roughly 37 times better, while 1% worse a day decays to almost nothing.
cards.apply: Choose one skill and find one small thing to do slightly better tomorrow. Repeat.

cards.text: Wind extinguishes a candle and energizes fire.
cards.meaning: Stress and volatility hurt fragile things and strengthen antifragile ones. The goal is to be the fire: set up so that shocks make you better, not just leave you standing.
cards.apply: Find one area (career, portfolio, routine) where a shock would wipe you out, and add a buffer or an option that benefits from disorder.

cards.text: Use a barbell strategy
cards.meaning: Instead of taking medium risk everywhere, put most resources in very safe positions and a small slice in high-upside bets. The downside is capped and the upside stays open.
cards.apply: Apply it to your time: keep your core work very reliable, and set aside a small weekly block for speculative projects.

cards.text: Prefer options over predictions
cards.meaning: Forecasting is unreliable, but you don't need to predict if you hold choices that pay off when things change. Optionality lets you benefit from what you couldn't foresee.
cards.apply: Before a big commitment, ask how you could keep the right to walk away or scale up later.

cards.text: Deep work is rare, and that makes it valuable
cards.meaning: Focused, distraction-free work produces the hard-to-copy results the economy rewards, yet most people spend their days in shallow email and meetings. That gap is an opportunity.
cards.apply: Block two 90-minute sessions this week with notifications off and protect them like client meetings.

cards.text: Switching tasks leaves attention residue
cards.meaning: When you switch tasks, part of your attention stays stuck on the previous one, so your thinking gets worse. Even a quick inbox check pays this tax.
cards.apply: Batch email and messages into set windows instead of checking them between focused tasks.

cards.text: The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
cards.meaning: Thoreau saw most people living by convention, working for things they don't value, and never questioning it. His experiment at Walden was a test of how little you need to live deliberately.
cards.apply: List three things you do mainly because they're expected of you, and decide whether to keep each one.

cards.text: Our life is frittered away by detail. Simplify, simplify.
cards.meaning: Complexity eats time and attention. Thoreau argues for cutting obligations and possessions down to what really matters.
cards.apply: Pick one area (subscriptions, recurring meetings, apps on your phone) and cut it by a third.

cards.text: Watch supply, not demand
cards.meaning: Marathon's capital cycle: high returns attract capital, new capacity floods in, and returns fall. Most analysts obsess over demand forecasts, but supply is easier to see coming and matters more.
cards.apply: For a sector you follow, chart industry capex growth for the last five years. A boom in spending is a warning sign, not a growth story.

cards.text: Low returns cure low returns
cards.meaning: When an industry earns poor returns, capital leaves, weak players exit or merge and capacity shrinks. That sets up the next recovery, often while sentiment is still gloomy.
cards.apply: Screen for industries where capex is falling and consolidation is under way. Those are where future returns improve.

cards.text: Judge managers by when they spend
cards.meaning: Value is destroyed by managers who build and acquire at the top of the cycle. The best invest when others retreat and return cash when assets are expensive.
cards.apply: Look at a company's last cycle: did it buy back stock and make acquisitions near the peak or the trough?

cards.text: Good management can sink great companies
cards.meaning: Incumbents fail not through stupidity but by doing what they're supposed to do: listening to their best customers and chasing higher margins. That rational behaviour makes them ignore disruptive technologies early on.
cards.apply: List the cheap, 'not good enough' products nibbling at the low end of an industry you cover. Ask which could improve into a real threat.

cards.text: Disruption starts at the bottom
cards.meaning: Disruptive products start out simpler, cheaper and worse, serving customers incumbents don't want. They improve until they're good enough for the mainstream, as with smaller disk drives and steel minimills.
cards.apply: When a company dismisses a rival as low-end, check how fast the rival's product is improving each year.

cards.text: Give the new bet its own house
cards.meaning: Christensen found incumbents succeed with disruptive technology when they set up a separate, small organisation whose costs and expectations fit a small, new market.
cards.apply: If you're testing something new at work, protect it from being judged by the core business's metrics.

cards.text: Chips are the new oil
cards.meaning: Miller argues semiconductors now underpin the global economy and military power the way oil did in the 20th century, and production is concentrated in a handful of companies and places.
cards.apply: For any tech or industrial company you follow, map which critical chips it depends on and who makes them.

cards.text: The industry runs through chokepoints
cards.meaning: Taiwan's TSMC makes most of the world's most advanced logic chips, and the Dutch firm ASML is the only maker of the EUV lithography machines needed to produce them. A few chokepoints carry enormous geopolitical risk.
cards.apply: When you assess supply-chain risk, flag every input with a single dominant supplier.

cards.text: Relentless scaling rewards giants
cards.meaning: Moore's Law, transistor counts doubling roughly every two years, drove costs down for decades. Keeping pace takes huge capex, which pushed the industry to consolidate into a few winners.
cards.apply: In capital-heavy industries, compare each player's capex with the cost of staying at the frontier. Laggards fall further behind every cycle.

cards.text: Capital allocation is the CEO's real job
cards.meaning: Thorndike studies eight CEOs, including Henry Singleton of Teledyne, Tom Murphy of Capital Cities and Warren Buffett, who far outperformed the market and their peers. What they shared wasn't charisma but a focus on where each dollar of cash flow went.
cards.apply: For a company you cover, add up 10 years of cash flow and show where it went: capex, M&A, buybacks, dividends, debt paydown.

cards.text: Buy back stock when it's cheap
cards.meaning: Singleton used Teledyne's cash to repurchase a large majority of its shares when the price was low. Buybacks at the right price can beat almost any other investment.
cards.apply: Next time a company announces a buyback, compare the repurchase price with your estimate of intrinsic value.

cards.text: Decentralize operations, centralize capital
cards.meaning: These CEOs ran lean headquarters, let unit managers run operations, and kept capital decisions at the top.
cards.apply: For an industrial conglomerate, check corporate overhead as a share of revenue and who decides on capital allocation.

cards.text: Output is set by the bottleneck
cards.meaning: Goldratt's Theory of Constraints, told as a novel about a struggling plant: a system can only produce as fast as its slowest step. Improving anything else doesn't raise output.
cards.apply: Map the steps in a process you run (a deal pipeline, a model build) and find where work piles up. Fix only that first.

cards.text: Measure throughput, not busyness
cards.meaning: The goal is to make money. Goldratt tracks throughput, inventory and operating expense. Keeping every machine busy can just pile up inventory without selling more.
cards.apply: When you look at a manufacturer, watch inventory growth against sales growth. Rising inventory can hide a slowdown.

cards.text: An hour lost at the bottleneck is lost for good
cards.meaning: Downtime at the constraint costs the whole system's output, while time saved elsewhere is often an illusion.
cards.apply: Protect your scarcest resource (often your own focus time) from interruptions first.

cards.text: Deregulation unleashed a brutal price war
cards.meaning: After the 1978 Airline Deregulation Act, airlines could set their own fares and routes. New entrants and fare wars followed, and many famous carriers went bankrupt.
cards.apply: When an industry deregulates or loses a barrier to entry, expect margins to compress before a new structure emerges.

cards.text: Airlines invented modern pricing
cards.meaning: The fight for survival produced tools now used everywhere: computer reservation systems like Sabre, yield management that prices each seat by demand, and frequent-flyer programmes such as American's AAdvantage (1981).
cards.apply: Ask how the companies you follow price: one list price, or dynamically by customer and timing? There's often hidden margin there.

cards.text: Perishable seats and fixed costs mean overcapacity
cards.meaning: An empty seat is worth nothing after takeoff, and most costs are fixed, so airlines are tempted to sell seats at any price above cash cost. That makes the industry prone to overcapacity and losses.
cards.apply: For an airline, compare unit cost (CASM excluding fuel) with peers and track industry capacity growth against demand.

cards.text: Oil is about power, not just energy
cards.meaning: Yergin traces how oil shaped the 20th century, from Standard Oil's empire to wars and the US oil embargo that factored into Japan's decision to go to war in 1941.
cards.apply: When you analyse a commodity producer, list the governments that can change its economics overnight.

cards.text: Boom and bust is built in
cards.meaning: Big discoveries create gluts and price crashes, so producers keep trying to control supply: Standard Oil, the Texas Railroad Commission, then OPEC.
cards.apply: Stress-test any materials or energy name at bottom-of-cycle prices, not today's.

cards.text: Supply shocks reorder the world
cards.meaning: The 1973 Arab oil embargo roughly quadrupled oil prices in months, triggering inflation and recession and shifting wealth and power to producers.
cards.apply: Identify one input your portfolio or business depends on and plan what you'd do if its price tripled.

cards.text: Buy when nobody else will
cards.meaning: Zell earned the nickname 'the Grave Dancer' by buying distressed, overbuilt real estate when others were fleeing. Contrarian timing, backed by analysis, was his edge.
cards.apply: Keep a watch list of property types or markets everyone hates right now and what price would make each attractive.

cards.text: Sell into froth
cards.meaning: In 2007 Zell sold Equity Office Properties to Blackstone for about $39 billion including debt, close to the market's peak.
cards.apply: Write down in advance what valuation or cap rate would make you a seller of your best asset, and honour it.

cards.text: Focus on the downside first
cards.meaning: Zell stresses understanding what you can lose before what you can make. Surviving the bad case is what lets you profit later.
cards.apply: For every deal, write the worst-case scenario in one paragraph and confirm you can survive it.

cards.text: A few outsiders saw it coming
cards.meaning: Michael Burry, Steve Eisman's team and the small fund Cornwall Capital bet against subprime mortgage bonds through credit default swaps while Wall Street kept buying.
cards.apply: When consensus is overwhelming, write the strongest bear case yourself. If you can't, you don't understand the trade.

cards.text: Complexity hid the risk
cards.meaning: Risky loans were pooled into bonds, then repackaged into CDOs, and rating agencies stamped much of it AAA. Each layer made the underlying risk harder to see.
cards.apply: When a product or structure is hard to explain, trace it back to the cash flows at the bottom.

cards.text: Read what others skip
cards.meaning: Burry's edge came from reading bond prospectuses and loan-level detail that almost nobody else bothered with.
cards.apply: Read one set of 10-K footnotes or loan documents in full this week, the parts most analysts skim.

title: This Time Is Different
author: Carmen M. Reinhart & Kenneth S. Rogoff

cards.text: 'This time is different' are dangerous words
cards.meaning: Studying eight centuries of financial crises, the authors find every boom was justified by new-era thinking that said the old rules no longer applied.
cards.apply: When you hear a new-paradigm argument for high valuations, look up how the last three versions of it ended.

cards.text: Debt buildups come before crises
cards.meaning: Big run-ups in borrowing, capital inflows and house prices are common warning signs before banking crises.
cards.apply: Track credit growth against GDP in the markets you invest in. Rapid acceleration is a yellow flag.

cards.text: Recovery after a banking crisis is slow
cards.meaning: Downturns after banking crises tend to be deep and long, with years of falling house prices and high unemployment.
cards.apply: If a banking crisis hits, plan for a multi-year recovery, not a quick V.

title: Archimedes
author: Life and ideas, via Plutarch and Vitruvius

cards.text: Give me a place to stand, and I will move the earth.
cards.meaning: Attributed to Archimedes by later writers like Pappus of Alexandria. He worked out the law of the lever: with the right lever and fulcrum, a small force can move an enormous load.
cards.apply: Find the lever in your work: the one skill, tool or relationship that multiplies everything else. Put an extra hour a week into it.

cards.text: Eureka: insight comes after deep immersion
cards.meaning: Vitruvius tells how Archimedes, stuck on whether King Hiero's crown was pure gold, noticed water rising as he got into the bath and saw how to measure volume by displacement. The breakthrough came from stepping away after soaking in the problem.
cards.apply: Load a hard problem in fully, then go for a walk or a workout. Keep a note open for when the answer arrives.

cards.text: Turn knowledge into defense
cards.meaning: Plutarch describes Archimedes' war machines (cranes, claws and catapults) holding off the Roman siege of Syracuse for about two years. Theory became practical power.
cards.apply: Take one idea you've learned recently and build something concrete from it this week: a model, a checklist, a tool.

cards.text: Test it instead of trusting authority
cards.meaning: For centuries people accepted Aristotle's claim that heavier objects fall faster. Galileo tested it, rolling balls down inclined planes, and showed that falling objects accelerate the same way regardless of weight (air resistance aside).
cards.apply: Pick one 'everyone knows' belief in your field and find the actual data behind it.

cards.text: Look through the new instrument
cards.meaning: In 1609–10 Galileo built improved telescopes and saw Jupiter's moons, mountains on the Moon and the phases of Venus, evidence that Earth wasn't the centre of everything. A new tool revealed what reasoning alone couldn't.
cards.apply: Spend an hour this week learning a tool your peers aren't using yet.

cards.text: Being right can cost you, and still win
cards.meaning: In 1633 the Inquisition forced Galileo to recant his support for a Sun-centred universe, and he spent the rest of his life under house arrest. His ideas prevailed anyway, and the Church formally acknowledged its error in 1992.
cards.apply: If your evidence-backed view is unpopular, write it down with your reasoning and date it. Let time judge.

cards.text: If I have seen further it is by standing on the shoulders of Giants.
cards.meaning: Newton wrote this to Robert Hooke in 1675. Even the greatest breakthroughs build on the work of others. Studying the masters is the fastest way to see further.
cards.apply: Before starting on a hard problem, find the three best people who've already tackled it and study how they did.

cards.text: Go away and think deeply
cards.meaning: When plague closed Cambridge in 1665–66, Newton went home to Woolsthorpe and, largely alone, laid the foundations of calculus, his theory of light and his ideas on gravitation.
cards.apply: Block one long, uninterrupted session each week for your hardest thinking: no phone, no email.

cards.text: Inertia rules projects and habits too
cards.meaning: Newton's first law says an object stays at rest or in motion unless a force acts on it. Habits and projects behave the same way: starting is the hardest part, and momentum carries you.
cards.apply: Shrink the first step of a stalled project until it takes five minutes, and do it today.

cards.text: Darwin's golden rule: note what proves you wrong
cards.meaning: In his autobiography Darwin says that whenever he met a fact that went against his theory, he wrote it down at once, because such facts slip from memory far faster than the ones that agree with you.
cards.apply: Keep a running 'disconfirming evidence' note for each investment thesis or big decision, and add to it immediately.

cards.text: 'Fittest' means best suited, not strongest
cards.meaning: Natural selection favours traits that suit the environment. The phrase 'survival of the fittest' came from Herbert Spencer, and 'fit' means a good match for conditions, not raw strength.
cards.apply: When your industry changes, ask which of your skills still fit and which you need to grow.

cards.text: Build the evidence before you go public
cards.meaning: Darwin spent about two decades collecting evidence before publishing On the Origin of Species in 1859, finally prompted by Alfred Russel Wallace reaching similar ideas. The weight of evidence is what made the book persuasive.
cards.apply: Before pitching a big idea, gather more evidence than you think you need, especially on its weakest point.

title: Scholars of the Islamic Golden Age
author: Baghdad, Cairo, Bukhara and beyond

cards.text: Ibn al-Haytham: question every authority
cards.meaning: Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040) wrote the Book of Optics, showed that we see because light enters the eye, and used controlled experiments to test his ideas. In his Doubts Concerning Ptolemy he argued a researcher should critically examine even the most revered authorities. He's often called a pioneer of the scientific method.
cards.apply: Take the source you trust most on a topic and write down three ways it could be wrong.

cards.text: Al-Khwarizmi: turn problems into procedures
cards.meaning: Working at Baghdad's House of Wisdom in the 9th century, al-Khwarizmi wrote the book on al-jabr that gave algebra its name, and his own name gave us the word 'algorithm'. He turned problem-solving into step-by-step methods anyone could follow.
cards.apply: Write a step-by-step procedure for one task you repeat every week, then streamline it.

cards.text: The House of Wisdom: collect the best ideas from everywhere
cards.meaning: In Abbasid Baghdad, scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and built on them, which helped make the city a world centre of science for centuries.
cards.apply: Read one book this month from a field or culture far outside your own and note what you can borrow.

cards.text: Ibn Sina: systematize what you know
cards.meaning: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037) organised the medical knowledge of his day into the Canon of Medicine, which stayed a standard textbook in European universities for centuries.
cards.apply: Turn your scattered notes on one subject into a single organised document you can reuse and share.

title: Science for Everyday Life
author: Ideas from Feynman, Pasteur, Ockham and physics

cards.text: The first principle: don't fool yourself
cards.meaning: In his 1974 Caltech commencement speech, 'Cargo Cult Science', Richard Feynman warned that you are the easiest person to fool. Real honesty means actively looking for what could make you wrong.
cards.apply: Before your next big decision, ask a sharp colleague to argue the opposite side as hard as they can.

cards.text: Chance favors only the prepared mind.
cards.meaning: Louis Pasteur said this in an 1854 lecture. Lucky discoveries happen to people who've done the groundwork to recognise an opportunity when it shows up.
cards.apply: Pick one area where you want 'luck' (a job, a deal, an idea) and do one hour of groundwork on it this week.

cards.text: Occam's razor: prefer the simpler explanation
cards.meaning: Named after the 14th-century friar William of Ockham: when two explanations fit the facts equally well, the one with fewer assumptions is usually the better bet.
cards.apply: When a thesis needs five things to go right, look for the simpler story the evidence also supports.

cards.text: Entropy: everything decays without upkeep
cards.meaning: The second law of thermodynamics says isolated systems drift toward disorder. Keeping anything orderly (health, relationships, a codebase, a model) takes continuous energy.
cards.apply: Put recurring maintenance on your calendar for the three things that matter most to you.

cards.text: If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it
cards.meaning: The learning method often named after Feynman: explain a topic in plain words as if to a beginner, find where you get stuck, then go back and fill those gaps.
cards.apply: Explain one concept from your work in a single paragraph with no jargon. Wherever you stumble, that's your gap.

cards.text: Veni, vidi, vici.
cards.meaning: 'I came, I saw, I conquered': according to Plutarch and Suetonius, Caesar's report to Rome after a lightning victory at Zela in 47 BC. Speed of action and brevity of message reinforced each other.
cards.apply: Write your next update in three short lines: what you did, what you found, what happened.

cards.text: The die is cast.
cards.meaning: Suetonius says Caesar said this ('alea iacta est') as he crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, an act that made civil war unavoidable. Once he'd decided, he committed fully, with no way back.
cards.apply: For a decision you've already made, remove the fallback option that keeps you half-committed.

cards.text: Speed is a weapon
cards.meaning: Caesar was famous for celeritas, rapid forced marches that put his legions in front of enemies before they were ready. Moving faster than opponents expect often decides the contest before it starts.
cards.apply: Find one thing you're waiting on that you could move forward today rather than next week.

cards.text: Clemency wins converts, but not everyone
cards.meaning: In the civil war Caesar pardoned many opponents, which brought defectors to his side. But some he spared, including Brutus and Cassius, later led his assassination in 44 BC.
cards.apply: Be generous with former rivals, but watch what people do over time rather than trusting a single gesture.

cards.text: Spot the gap and strike first
cards.meaning: At the Battle of Uhud in 625, Khalid, then commanding cavalry for Mecca, saw archers leave their hill post and attacked through the opening. He later became Islam's most famous general, called Sayf Allah, 'the Sword of God', and tradition holds he was never defeated.
cards.apply: In a negotiation or competitive situation, watch for the moment the other side drops its guard, and be ready to act on it.

cards.text: Make the move no one thinks possible
cards.meaning: According to the chronicles, in 634 Khalid led his army from Iraq to Syria across a waterless desert, reportedly using camels as water reserves, and appeared where the Byzantines didn't expect him.
cards.apply: List the options your competitors assume are impossible, and test whether one actually is.

cards.text: Mission before ego
cards.meaning: Caliph Umar removed Khalid from supreme command at the height of his success. Khalid kept fighting under his replacement, Abu Ubayda, including at the decisive Battle of Yarmouk in 636.
cards.apply: The next time you're passed over or overruled, decide how to keep contributing to the result instead of withdrawing.

cards.text: Hold the powerful to account
cards.meaning: As caliph (634–644), Umar was known for auditing his governors' wealth and dismissing those who enriched themselves in office, even successful ones.
cards.apply: Set clear, checkable standards for yourself and anyone reporting to you, and review them on a schedule.

cards.text: Build systems that outlast you
cards.meaning: Under Umar the state set up the diwan (a registry for pay and pensions), adopted the Hijri calendar, and founded garrison cities like Basra and Kufa. These institutions ran a rapidly expanding empire.
cards.apply: Turn one thing that depends on you personally into a documented process someone else could run.

cards.text: Live simply with power
cards.meaning: Early accounts describe Umar wearing patched clothes and walking the streets of Medina at night to see how ordinary people were living.
cards.apply: Spend time each month where the work actually happens (a site visit, a customer call) instead of relying only on reports.

cards.text: Unite before you fight
cards.meaning: Salahuddin spent years bringing Egypt and Syria under one leadership before taking on the Crusader states. A united base came before the big campaign.
cards.apply: Before a major push at work, line up the stakeholders and resources you need. Don't launch with a divided team.

cards.text: Mercy is strength
cards.meaning: After defeating the Crusaders at Hattin, he retook Jerusalem in 1187 and let much of the population ransom themselves and leave, a sharp contrast with the massacre when the Crusaders took the city in 1099. His reputation for honour spread even among his enemies.
cards.apply: When you win a dispute, be generous with the other side. Reputation compounds.

cards.text: Give away more than you keep
cards.meaning: His biographer Baha ad-Din reports that Salahuddin gave so much away that, when he died in 1193, he left too little money even for his own funeral.
cards.apply: Find one way this month to share credit, time or resources more generously than usual.

cards.text: Asabiyyah: cohesion wins
cards.meaning: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) argued that groups with strong solidarity, often forged by hard desert life, conquer comfortable settled societies. Group cohesion, asabiyyah, drives the rise of dynasties.
cards.apply: Judge a team or company by how much its people trust and back each other, not only by its resources.

cards.text: Comfort erodes strength in three generations
cards.meaning: He observed that dynasties typically last about three generations: founders are tough, successors maintain, and their heirs, raised in luxury, lose the cohesion that built the state.
cards.apply: Look at a family business or founder-led company you know. Which generation is it in, and is the founding discipline still there?

cards.text: Lower taxes can raise revenue
cards.meaning: He noted that young dynasties collect large revenues from low tax rates, while declining ones raise rates and collect less, an idea later compared to the Laffer curve.
cards.apply: When a company raises prices, check whether total revenue actually grows or volume falls away.

title: The Warrior's Way
author: Sayings and codes from warrior traditions

cards.text: Be a warrior in a garden, not a gardener in a war
cards.meaning: Train for hardship in peaceful times so you're never caught unprepared. Being capable gives you the choice to be gentle; being helpless leaves you none. The saying is often credited to Sun Tzu or a Japanese proverb, but it doesn't appear in those texts and its origin is unknown.
cards.apply: Pick one capability (fitness, savings, a hard skill) and build it now, while nothing is forcing you to.

cards.text: Come and take them.
cards.meaning: 'Molon labe': Plutarch records this as the Spartan king Leonidas's reply when Xerxes demanded the Greeks lay down their arms at Thermopylae in 480 BC. Defiance backed by readiness.
cards.apply: Decide what you won't give up under pressure (your standards, your boundaries) before the pressure arrives.

cards.text: Forge for a thousand days, polish for ten thousand
cards.meaning: In The Book of Five Rings, Miyamoto Musashi, the undefeated duellist who was also a painter and calligrapher, says real mastery takes years of daily training, forging and then polishing.
cards.apply: Choose one skill and commit to a small daily practice you'll keep for a year.

cards.text: You become what you repeatedly do
cards.meaning: Aristotle argued that character is built by habit: we become just by doing just acts, and brave by doing brave acts. The famous line 'We are what we repeatedly do' is actually Will Durant's summary of this idea, not Aristotle's own words.
cards.apply: Name a trait you want and the smallest action that expresses it. Do it every day this week.

cards.text: One swallow does not make a summer, nor does one day.
cards.meaning: For Aristotle, a flourishing life (eudaimonia) comes from virtuous activity sustained over a whole life, not a single good moment or lucky break.
cards.apply: Judge your progress over months, not days. Review the last quarter, not yesterday.

cards.text: Find the golden mean
cards.meaning: Virtue sits between two extremes: courage between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and extravagance. The right point depends on the situation.
cards.apply: For a trait you overdo (caution, ambition, agreeableness), name its opposite extreme and move one step toward the middle.
